name: Wendy Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run Cross Lanes, which is my family's farm: sixty suckler cows, some sheep, a few fields of potatoes and veg, and the farm shop by the road. Since Dad's knee operation I'm the one who decides what gets planted and what goes in the shop. A day is feeding at six, then the shop opens at nine and I'm in and out between the till and the field. In the evening I use AI to plan the shop orders and write our posts, which my mum thinks is witchcraft.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the money work for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Badly, if I'm honest. I take a small wage, less than I'd get managing someone else's farm, because every spare pound goes back into the shop freezer or the fencing. I've got about a fortnight of savings. Jun, my partner, is a nurse, so his wage pays most of our rent on the cottage, which I feel bad about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. So I keep using it for shop orders and that's it. Fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that got sold as a miracle. It saves me an hour a night on stock orders and writes better shop posts than I do, but it never touched the cows. I'd also say people should be glad farm jobs didn't vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a little bit sad. I'd hoped it might help small farms like ours compete with the big supermarket chains, like a cheap manager in the back office. If nothing changes, we're still a tiny shop fighting a giant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am and push the AI tools further in the shop: stock forecasts, a simple online order page, maybe a veg box scheme. I'd join the local food co-op and try to get three or four farms selling together. Nothing big, because there's no money for big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of itch. I like change, and this one would be a damp squib.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try to get farms selling together. Why that, rather than going it alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because alone we're too small for anything. If four farms share a van and an online shop, we're suddenly worth delivering for. My dad would hate it, he likes doing things his way, but the numbers don't lie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum make of a veg box scheme?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd moan about the packing and then end up doing most of it, and loving it. She already talks to every customer for twenty minutes. I'd have to give her a headset.

S0.say: I'd say it's a decent tool sold as a miracle: it saves me an hour a night on orders and writes better posts than me, but never touched the cows. People should be glad farm jobs didn't vanish.
S0.think: I'd be a bit sad, because I hoped it would help small farms compete with the big chains. If nothing changes, we're still a tiny shop fighting a giant.
S0.do: Pushes AI further in the shop with stock forecasts, an online order page and a veg box scheme. Joins the local food co-op and tries to get three or four farms selling together.
S0.feel: Calm with an itch, because she likes change and this would be a damp squib.
S0.quote: If nothing changes, we're still a tiny shop fighting a giant.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy already uses AI daily and is the only one so far who sounds disappointed it would stop. She thinks like a co-operative builder, pooling small farms against big buyers. The money gap is clear: her partner's nursing wage carries their rent, and she feels guilty about it. Her family, especially her dad, is a brake she plans around rather than fights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now this one I'm actually excited about. It's like the tools I use at night, but they finally get out into the field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small farms should get in early and not leave it to the big estates. I'd be the one at the farmers' meeting saying we should share a weeding robot between six farms. I'd also say the savings should go into wages and local food, not into some investor's pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one could be the making of us. If a robot does the weeding and AI does the paperwork, I get my evenings back and the shop can grow. My only fear is the debt, because new kit costs money we don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd set up a machinery-sharing group with the farms on our lane, so nobody has to buy a robot alone. I'd apply for every small-farm tech grant going, and I'd learn to run the weeding robot myself instead of paying a contractor. The shop would get a proper online ordering system by spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a little knot in my stomach about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our neighbour Gareth, who does contract hedge-cutting and spraying. That's the kind of work a robot does first. I'd want him in the sharing group, running the machines, rather than watching them go past his gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your dad would resist. How would you bring him round?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't argue. I'd borrow a robot for a week, let it weed the carrots, and leave the results in the shop window. He's stubborn but he's not daft.

S1.say: I'd say small farms should get in early and not leave it to the big estates, and we should share a weeding robot between six farms. The savings should go into wages and local food, not investors.
S1.think: I think this could be the making of us, giving me my evenings back and letting the shop grow. My only fear is debt, because new kit costs money we don't have.
S1.do: Sets up a machinery-sharing group with neighbouring farms and applies for small-farm tech grants. Learns to run the weeding robot herself and gets the shop a proper online ordering system by spring.
S1.feel: Excited, with a small knot in her stomach about money.
S1.quote: He's stubborn but he's not daft.
S1.fieldNote: This is the one scenario where Wendy sounds genuinely excited. Her plan is collective, a machinery-sharing group, which fits her progressive outlook without slowing her down. She thought immediately about a neighbour whose contracting work is at risk and wants him inside the change. Her tactic with her dad, showing results rather than arguing, was telling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay, that's a lot faster than I'm comfortable with, and I'm usually the one who likes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public rules and public money right now, not in five years. If AI and robots can do almost any job, the gains have to be shared, through tax and a basic income. I'd be posting that every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think the farm survives as a business. Big automated farms will grow food so cheap we can't compete, and the shop's customers might have no wages to spend. What might survive is the land, and what people want from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd sit down with Mum, Dad and Jun and work out what we'd keep if the business failed: the house, the land, the animals we love. I'd try to turn the shop into a community food hub, where people can come and buy cheap or swap work for food. And I'd be at every council and farmers' union meeting pushing for land to stay with local people, not get bought up by robot farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but also a bit fired up. It's frightening, and it's also a fight I'd want to be in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means there's no time to grow into it, only to protect what we have. With five or ten years I'd be building, sharing robots, growing the shop. With two years I'd be digging in and trying to keep the land in the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Does any part of you welcome this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small part, yes, and I feel guilty saying it. A world where machines grow the food could mean nobody goes hungry. But I can't see how we get there without a lot of families losing their farms first, and one of them might be mine.

S2.say: I'd say we need public rules and public money right now, not in five years. If AI can do almost any job, the gains must be shared through tax and a basic income.
S2.think: I don't think the farm survives as a business against cheap automated farms and customers with no wages. What might survive is the land and what people want from it.
S2.do: Sits down with her parents and partner to decide what to keep if the business fails. Tries to turn the shop into a community food hub and campaigns at council and union meetings to keep land with local people.
S2.feel: Alarmed but fired up, frightened and wanting to be in the fight.
S2.quote: With two years I'd be digging in and trying to keep the land in the family.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most tech-eager of these farmers is shaken by two years. Wendy's response is to protect the land and turn the shop into a community food hub, not to run. She admitted a guilty hope that machine-grown food could end hunger. Her blame is diffuse; her demand is shared gains through tax and basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a real window. I can work with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to make sure small farms get a share of this, if the government acts now. I'd push for grants so farms can buy robots together, and for a fund to help farm workers move into new roles. Online I'd say it's coming, so let's shape it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is my best case. I could get the sharing group running, automate the boring work, and turn the shop into something that sells the experience, not just the food. People will want to see where food comes from even if robots grow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the machinery group going with two or three farms and borrow or rent our first robot. I'd learn to manage the robots myself and use AI for the shop books. By year two I'd start farm visits and school trips, which bring in money that a robot farm can't copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the useful kind. I'd have a list and I'd be ticking it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Farm visits sound good, but you've got a fortnight of savings. How do you pay for the start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grants, mostly, and a bit of borrowing against the shop. Jun would hate me borrowing, and he'd be right to worry. I'd keep it small: a toilet block, some signs, a field for parking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gareth with five years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the robots now, this winter, and come and run ours. In five years there'll be a lot of farms needing someone who can fix one at short notice. That's a better living than hedge-cutting.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for small farms to get a share of this if the government acts now. I'd push for shared robot grants and a fund to help farm workers move into new roles.
S3.think: I think five years is my best case: I could automate the boring work and turn the shop into something that sells the experience as well as the food. People will want to see where food comes from.
S3.do: Starts a machinery-sharing group and rents its first robot in year one, learning to manage it herself. Adds farm visits and school trips by year two, paid for with grants and a small loan against the shop.
S3.feel: Anxious in a useful way, with a list she would be ticking off.
S3.quote: People will want to see where food comes from even if robots grow it.
S3.fieldNote: Five years puts Wendy back in building mode. Her bet is that the human, visible side of farming becomes the product. She admitted the borrowing would worry her partner, a real tension in a household with a fortnight's savings. She again thought about her neighbour Gareth and offered him a concrete path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that I'd actually enjoy it, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the version where we can do it right, so no excuses. I'd want farm colleges teaching robot management now and land rules that stop big companies hoovering up small farms. Publicly I'd be the cheerful one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine, probably better than fine. I'm young, I like tech, and ten years is time to turn Cross Lanes into a small, smart farm with a busy shop and visitors. My real worry is everyone else on our lane who doesn't move as fast as me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start the sharing group and do a part-time course in farm robotics at the agricultural college. I'd grow the online shop and start saving properly, maybe a hundred a month, once the shop's margins improve. Jun and I might finally talk about buying a small place, because I'd feel I had a future to build on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Hopeful, with a bit of guilt that it's easier for me than for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why feel guilty?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's easier for me. I'm 27, I like screens, my family owns land. Gareth is 50 and rents his yard. Ten years for me is a runway; for him it's a slow goodbye.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing on an ordinary Tuesday in 2036, if it went well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking the robots' overnight work on a tablet over breakfast, then walking the cows because I'd still want to. Then a school group at ten, the shop at lunch, and my mum telling the kids the same story about the bull that got out in 1998.

S4.say: I'd say this is the version we can do right, so there are no excuses. Farm colleges should teach robot management now and land rules should stop big companies swallowing small farms.
S4.think: I think I'd be fine or better, turning the farm into a small smart farm with a busy shop and visitors. My real worry is everyone on our lane who doesn't move as fast as me.
S4.do: Starts the sharing group and a part-time farm robotics course in year one. Grows the online shop, saves about a hundred a month once margins improve, and talks with her partner about buying a small home.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, with some guilt that it's easier for her than for others.
S4.quote: Ten years for me is a runway; for him it's a slow goodbye.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Wendy is calm and even happy, and she named her advantage plainly: young, tech-friendly, from a land-owning family. The guilt about a neighbour who rents his yard was sincere. Her picture of a good day in 2036 still includes walking the cows by choice. Family plans, a home with Jun, only appear in this scenario.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would hit before small farms like ours had any chance to adapt, and the land could end up with whoever has the most robots. What would help is public money for small farms to share machines, plus rules that stop land being bought up, and a basic income so the shop's customers still have money to spend.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the other people on the lane. I'll probably be fine in most of these, but Gareth and the older workers around here won't be, and they're the ones who taught me. I'd want any plan to start with them.

headlineQuote: People will want to see where food comes from even if robots grow it.
portrait: Wendy Alvarez is 27 and runs her family's mixed farm and roadside farm shop, taking a small wage and leaning on her partner Jun's nursing pay for the rent. She uses AI every night for shop orders and posts and is the most excited of anyone about robots, as long as small farms share them. In the slower scenarios she plans machinery-sharing groups, an online shop and farm visits; in the two-year picture she switches to protecting the family land and turning the shop into a community food hub. She keeps coming back to her neighbour Gareth and feels guilty that change would be easier for her than for others.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because small farms would have no time to adapt and land could end up with whoever owns the most robots.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for small farms to share machines, rules against land being bought up, and a basic income so local customers can still spend.
